passage: I've seen the proposal to switch our inventory counts to barcode scanners. This plant has counted stock on clipboards since my grandfather worked the line, and we've gotten by fine. If it worked for three generations, it'll work for us. Let's get the forklifts moving.
cue: If it worked for three generations, it'll work for us.
explanation: The supervisor rejects scanners because clipboards have been used for generations. Long use shows the method survived, not that it's as accurate or efficient as the alternative.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: He isn't pointing to how many plants use clipboards now; he's pointing to how long this one has.

passage: Westbrook football has been played on Friday nights under the lights since 1962. My dad played on that field, I played on it, my son plays on it now. Moving games to Saturday afternoons to save on 'electricity costs' is ridiculous. Some things you just don't change. Go Herons!
cue: Some things you just don't change.
explanation: Earl rejects the cost-saving move because Friday games go back decades in his family and town. That history means a lot to him, but it doesn't answer the electricity cost question.

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Earl's reason is how long the custom has lasted, not how many people currently favor Friday games.

title: Re: Spring fundraiser ideas
passage: Hi everyone, a few parents suggested replacing the wrapping-paper sale with an online donation drive, and I appreciate the thought. Online would save volunteer hours, that's true. But the wrapping-paper sale has been how Maple Ridge raises money for nearly thirty years, and I don't see a reason to drop something that's part of who we are. Deb
cue: has been how Maple Ridge raises money for nearly thirty years
explanation: Deborah grants that the online drive would save volunteer time, then keeps the sale mainly because it's a thirty-year habit. Its age doesn't show it raises more money or is worth the hours.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Nothing here is about what's natural; Deborah's reason is simply how long the sale has been a school custom.

title: Some recipes shouldn't be touched
passage: The new owners at Odile's Diner added oat milk, a veggie hash and online ordering. Food came out fast and the hash was honestly tasty. But they've changed the pancake batter, which has been on this menu since 1958. I didn't even order them. You don't mess with a recipe that's lasted that long. Three stars.
cue: You don't mess with a recipe that's lasted that long.
explanation: Clement docks the diner for changing a decades-old recipe without even tasting the new pancakes. A recipe's age doesn't tell you whether the new version is better or worse.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Clement isn't objecting to anything artificial; he objects purely because the old recipe had lasted so long.

source: Hal Brunner · Osterbrook garden club talk
passage: Folks ask whether planting by the moon's phases actually works. My family has farmed this valley for four generations, and every one of them sowed root crops on the waning moon. That kind of knowledge, tested season after season, doesn't need a lab study to back it up. I'll be handing out this year's planting calendar at the door.
cue: That kind of knowledge, tested season after season, doesn't need a lab study to back it up.
explanation: Hal treats four generations of habit as proof that moon planting works. Repeating a practice isn't the same as testing it; without comparing results, the 'testing' is just tradition.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_nature: Hal's case isn't that moon planting is natural; it's that his family has done it for generations.

passage:
Grace: Survey says 72% of staff want to drop the business-casual dress code. Most client meetings are on video now anyway.
Hector: Before we scrap it, remember it's been in place since the firm opened in 1984. Policies that survive that long usually exist for good reasons, even if nobody remembers them. I'd keep it.
Grace: Do we know what the reasons were?
cue: Policies that survive that long usually exist for good reasons, even if nobody remembers them.
explanation: Hector sounds cautious, but he treats the dress code's age as proof it's justified without naming any reason. Grace's question is the right one: what was it for, and does that still apply?

whyNot.fal_bandwagon: Hector doesn't appeal to what most firms do; he appeals to how long this policy has lasted.

passage: People ask why we still use a 40-year-old wood-fired oven when a convection oven would be cheaper to run. We tried one for a month last winter: crust complaints tripled and our Saturday sellouts stopped. So the old oven stays, and not for nostalgia's sake. The bread is measurably better in it.
cue: We tried one for a month last winter: crust complaints tripled and our Saturday sellouts stopped.
explanation: The bakery keeps its old oven because of a real test: when it switched, complaints rose and sales fell. The reason is results, not age.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: The bakery doesn't keep the oven because it's old; it keeps it because a direct comparison showed better results.

title: Re: Removing the Dover St. turn restriction
passage: Before we remove the 'no left turn, 7 to 9 a.m.' sign on Dover Street because it 'has been there forever,' I pulled the history. It was added in 1998 after five crashes in two years at that corner, all during school drop-off. The school is still there and morning traffic has grown. The reason for the rule still holds, so I'd keep it.
cue: I pulled the history. It was added in 1998 after five crashes in two years
explanation: Maya checks why the rule exists and whether that reason still applies today. The rule survives because its safety purpose remains, not because it's old.

whyNot.fal_appeal_to_tradition: Maya doesn't defend the sign for its age; she finds its original safety reason and shows it still applies.
